newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Five dead in Nigerian Moslem clashes with police.
newsitem.headline: Five dead in Nigerian Moslem clashes with police.

text.p: Three Moslems and two policemen were killed in the northern Nigerian city of Kaduna on Wednesday when Shi'ite Moslems clashed with police, a Moslem group said.

A police spokeswoman told Reuters by telephone from Kaduna that two policemen were killed, but said she had no information on reports that three Moslems had been shot dead by riot police in Kaduna central market.
The clashes came after demonstrations by Shi'ite Moslems in Kaduna against the detention of their leaders. At the demonstrations police fired teargas to disperse the protesters.
"The police shot three of our people dead at the central market where two of their men were lynched by the mob," a member of the Shi'ite Moslem Brotherhood said by telephone from Kaduna.

Police in the mainly Moslem north, scene of bloody religious riots in the past, have been on alert over an ultimatum given by the Shi'ite group after its leader Ibrahim Yakub El-Zak-Zaky and others were arrested what police called for security reasons.
On Saturday the Shi'ites Moslem Brotherhood said 14 people had been killed in clashes with police at the weekend following El-Zak-Zaky's arrest but police deny there were deaths.
"We are concerned about Sheikh Zaky's health in detention," the Shi'ite member said.
Witnesses said more than 1,000 protesters were dispersed in Kaduna when the Moslems took to the streets for the second time in as many weeks over the detention of the sheikh.
"Anti-riot police men were out in full force to stop the demonstration," said a journalist from Kaduna.

At a news conference in Kaduna on Monday, Police Commissioner Yakubu Shaibu urged the public to disregard the ultimatum that said there would be trouble if El-Zak-Zaky and the others were not released by Wednesday.
Last month three people were killed in a clash between rival Moslem sects in Kano, the region's biggest city.
Moslems, predominantly Sunni, make up roughly half of Nigeria's 100 million people.
The police spokeswoman said calm had been restored in Kaduna and people were going about their businessnes normally.
"The rioters have been dispersed," she said, adding that the protest had not spread to other areas.

The protests pose a major challenge for the military rulers of Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation, which has been in crisis since June 1993 when the army annulled a presidential election to restore democracy.
A spokesman for the Shi'ite Moslem Brotherhood said their demonstration had nothing to do with the annulled poll.
"Of course our leader is preaching for a better Nigeria but this is not about the annulment," he said.
